source.title: The Salvation Army USA, 2026 National Annual Report: Financial Summary & Statistical Highlights (fiscal year ended 30 September 2025)
source.page: p. 23, Unaudited Combined Statement of Activities

rows.explainer: The Adult Rehabilitation Centers' whole cost: the residential recovery programme and the thrift stores that fund it (the Western Territory's audited functional-expense statement shows the line is mostly salaries and occupancy, with almost no direct assistance, which is the stores' profile). Read by both of our Salvation Army models (the US services and the overseas work), so the two always split the combined US accounts in full.

rows.label: Share of rehabilitation expenses that is the recovery programme itself (not the stores)
rows.explainer: No published split, so a judgment from three cross-checks. (1) Sales to the public were $553.2M in fiscal 2025 (p. 23); if store sales roughly cover the stores' own costs, the rest of the rehabilitation line, $186M or 25%, is the programme. (2) Beds × cost: the Eastern Territory runs 26 centres with 2,049 beds (saconnects.org, January 2026), so about 108 rehabilitation centres nationally hold roughly 8,500 beds; at $40-80 a bed-day for a work-therapy residence that is $125-250M, 17-34% of the line. (3) The one territory with public audited accounts, the Western, had sales to the public of $131.4M against a rehabilitation line of $150.1M in fiscal 2023 (statements pp. 5-6), which by the logic of (1) leaves 12.5%. Range 10-40%. Read by both of our Salvation Army models (the US services and the overseas work), so the two always split the combined US accounts in full.

rows.explainer: No split is published. 67 day care centres with 17,617 participants at sliding fees of a few thousand dollars a year would collect $20-80M of the $167M; camps, Kroc memberships and residents' rent the rest. 30% (15-50%). rows.label: Territories' other support for the international Salvation Army, fiscal 2025
rows.explainer: The territories also send 'world services support' abroad (the Western Territory $8.1M in fiscal 2023 and $15.9M in 2022, statements note 19), roughly $33M nationally at four times the Western figure; about $13M of the territories' giving goes to SAWSO (Give.org: contributions from the territories $13.1M), already in its expenses. The rest, $20M ($5-45M), funds the international Army's work overseas. The world-services money goes to International Headquarters' Self-Denial fund, which distributes it by need to the territories that can't pay their own way; the Canadian territory describes it as funding 'vital infrastructure resources that enable territories worldwide to carry out their mission' (salvationist.ca, Partners in Mission 2026 bulletin). Read by both of our Salvation Army models (the US services and the overseas work), so the two always split the combined US accounts in full.
